value.title: AI harm shifted from failures to misuse after ChatGPT
value.sentence: Malicious Actors & Misuse rose from 12% to 52% of MIT-labelled incidents after 30 Nov 2022, the largest shift in the risk-domain mix (Cramer's V 0.52; themes V 0.51).
value.limitation: Reported incidents only; MIT coverage is lower after the cut-off (78% vs 98%) and AIID's editorial intake changed over the same years.

value.title: 5 of 12 risk themes are emerging
value.sentence: Deepfake videos and hoaxes, hallucinated legal citations, deepfake impersonation scams, AI nude images in schools and AI election disinformation all grow significantly as a share of incidents (Mann-Kendall with Benjamini-Hochberg, 2015-2025).
value.limitation: Eleven complete years give little power; shares describe the database, not the real-world frequency of harm.

value.title: One in six recent incidents repeats a known failure, and search finds the precedent
value.sentence: 17% of incidents since 2024 have an editor-linked earlier precedent, and searching only earlier incidents puts it in the top 5 for 76% of them; at depth 3 our search scores MRR 0.45 against 0.034 for AIID's built-in suggestions.
value.limitation: Editors link only some incidents, so the share with a precedent is a lower bound and the search is scored on linked incidents only.

value.title: The AI-generated labels are usable but about 1 in 7 is doubtful
value.sentence: Editor-linked similar incidents share an MIT domain 75% of the time against 30% by chance, and the discrimination label agrees substantially with human CSETv1 annotation (kappa 0.74), yet confident learning estimates 15% of labels are wrong.
value.limitation: Human fields map only partially onto MIT domains and cover pre-2024 incidents; confident learning inherits the classifier's own errors.

value.title: Deepfake, scam and election harms concentrate around the big platforms
value.sentence: 3 of the 5 emerging themes concentrate in network community 1, where 92%-96% of their incidents involve its entities (about 1.6 times the rate for all incidents), with Meta and YouTube as the most central allegedly involved organisations.
value.limitation: Organisations are alleged deployers or developers, centrality reflects how often they are reported (not blame), and communities depend on a few hub entities.
